guides.name: get-ui-principle
guides.title: Visual foundations
guides.text:
Use semantic color and verify contrast
1. Map colors to roles such as foreground, surface, border, action and danger. Use the existing token names rather than scattering brand hex values through components.
2. For WCAG AA, ordinary text needs 4.5:1 contrast; qualifying large text needs 3:1. Required graphical control boundaries and focus indications generally need 3:1 against adjacent colors.
3. Pair color-coded status with text or a meaningful symbol. Disabled styling must remain understandable even where contrast exceptions apply.
4. Calculate contrast for the rendered foreground and composited background in each state. A palette swatch does not establish contrast on gradients, photos or translucent surfaces.

Verify: Check actual light/dark, focus, selected, hover, error and loading pairs. Record uncertain backgrounds rather than inventing a passing ratio.

Make the current task clear
1. Choose the information a visitor needs first, then place the task title, result or decision ahead of secondary detail. A navigation label does not replace a screen title.
2. Use position, type size, weight and spacing to establish order. Reserve the strongest action treatment for the action that advances this task.
3. Keep headings close to the content they name and use a larger gap between separate groups. If everything has equal emphasis, remove decoration before adding more.

Verify: View the screen at reduced size and in grayscale. Explain its purpose and next action without reading every paragraph.

Use readable, purposeful typography
1. Use the product's existing font family and a limited set of sizes and weights. Include system fallbacks and verify the chosen font actually loads.
2. Give body prose comfortable line height and line length; allow text to grow without clipping containers. Keep headings in a logical semantic order.
3. Use tabular numerals for comparable quantities, show units beside values and avoid letter spacing that harms small text.
4. Prefer natural wrapping. Do not hard-code a line break that becomes awkward in another language or at another viewport width.

Verify: Read the interface with the fallback font, 200% text zoom, long translated labels and a narrow viewport.

guides.name: get-ux-principle
guides.title: Forms and recovery
guides.text:
Make payment commitments explicit
1. Show the items, quantities, currency, taxes, shipping and final total before payment. Explain recurring charges and renewal terms beside the commitment.
2. Preserve cart and entered data through validation or payment failure. Use safe retry and reconcile uncertain payment outcomes before asking the buyer to pay again.
3. Offer a clear way to edit the order and use appropriate address, autofill and input modes. Do not preselect an optional paid addition.

Verify: Test declined payment, changed shipping cost, lost connection and duplicate submission with server-confirmed order state.

Help buyers narrow a product list
1. Show comparable product names, imagery, prices and availability. Include variant or pack information when it changes the apparent price.
2. Use filters that match buyer decisions, label active filters and make clearing them straightforward. Show a useful result count after filtering.
3. Preserve list position and filter state when the buyer visits a detail page and returns. Keep sort order separate from filtering.

Verify: Find a product using multiple filters, inspect its detail and return to the same list state on mobile.

Keep forms understandable and recoverable
1. Ask for information required for the immediate task, with visible labels and useful defaults. Explain formats, units and unfamiliar requirements before submission.
2. Validate when the user can act on feedback; avoid treating every incomplete keystroke as an error. Keep entered values after a failed submission.
3. Place a specific message beside the field and link a submission error summary to affected inputs. Announce status changes without moving focus unpredictably.

Verify: Submit missing and invalid values, recover from a server error and complete the form with a keyboard.

guides.name: get-motion-guide
guides.title: Motion and media
guides.text:
# Motion Guides matching "motion accessibility captions"

## Make the film understandable without audio (88% match)

1. Caption spoken information accurately and provide an accessible transcript where useful. Keep essential product information available without relying on sound.
2. Use readable caption contrast, line length and placement. Do not cover the control or result the viewer needs to follow.
3. Avoid rapid flashing and consider motion-sensitive viewers. Keep optional background sound below speech and respect export requirements.

Verify: Watch muted at delivery size, read the captions through each transition and check that essential visual context remains visible.

---

## Use one visual system across a product film (31% match)

1. Use the product's actual typography, color, control shapes and movement tokens. Keep the visual language consistent between title cards and product shots.
2. Choose motion that explains the task narrative. Do not imply shipped interactions or results that the product does not support.
3. Define output format, frame rate, readable type sizes and caption placement before authoring compositions.

Verify: Review representative frames at delivery resolution and confirm the product depiction is truthful and text remains legible.

---

## Review frames and the completed encoding (44% match)

1. Inspect selected frames around cuts, interaction triggers, text reveals and endings. Check clipping, fonts, imagery and source-state accuracy.
2. Play the full encoded file to check pacing, audio, captions and transitions. Static frames alone cannot establish smooth motion or sync.
3. Record the exact composition, props, assets and render settings used. Changes after review require checking the affected output again.

Verify: Verify both sampled frames and the final file, with muted playback and the intended delivery player.

---

## Compose for the delivery format (22% match)

1. Choose resolution, aspect ratio, frame rate and duration for the destination. Keep essential text and actions away from expected player or platform overlays.
2. Recompose important content for each format rather than cropping a widescreen composition blindly into a vertical frame.
3. Use integer frame boundaries for deterministic cuts. Verify the final encoding and audio behavior against destination requirements.

Verify: Inspect the complete frame at actual delivery size for each format, including captions and platform overlay areas.

Next: call `find-design-system` with the product's description. If no person is there to choose, take the top match and say which one you took. Then call `get-design-system-kit` to install it.

guides.name: get-react-native-guide
guides.title: React Native
guides.text:
# React Native Guides matching "accessible forms theme"

## Evaluate native Expo UI against requirements (44% match)

1. Check the currently installed Expo SDK and the library's platform support before selecting a native UI package. Do not assume a component exists on both iOS and Android.
2. Use native primitives where they improve interaction consistency, and keep business state outside platform-specific rendering.
3. Provide an accessible equivalent when a component or platform capability is unavailable. Verify the library's current API in its official documentation.

Verify: Build for each supported platform and test theme, accessibility and unsupported capability handling.

---

## Keep mobile chat readable under updates (22% match)

1. Keep the composer visible above the keyboard and respect safe-area insets. Preserve scroll position when messages arrive unless the user is already following the latest message.
2. Use stable message IDs, explicit sending/failure states and safe retry to avoid duplicates. Do not replace the entire list for a small update.
3. Announce incoming content proportionately and provide accessible timestamps and author context. Preserve drafted text across temporary interruption.

Verify: Test long messages, keyboard changes, failed sends, pagination and incoming messages while reading older history.

---

## Build with native platform constraints (22% match)

1. Use the app's established navigation, theme and state ownership. Respect safe-area insets and use platform controls where their behavior fits.
2. Provide accessibility labels, roles and state; test Dynamic Type or font scaling, screen readers and comfortable touch targets on devices.
3. Model loading, empty, error and offline states. Use virtualized lists for substantial data and stable keys to preserve item identity.

Verify: Run the task on both supported platforms with a virtual keyboard, large text and a slow connection.

Next: call `find-design-system` with the product's description. If no person is there to choose, take the top match and say which one you took. Then call `get-design-system-kit` to install it.

Check the screen on a device before you report it done:

1. Build and run the app in a simulator or on a device. A typecheck alone is not a build.
2. Take a screenshot of every state you built: empty, selected, disabled and dark mode.
3. Read each screenshot. Every label shows once and reads clearly: no text drawn twice, no button whose label matches its fill, no clipped or overlapping text, no chart or card spilling over its neighbour. Fix what fails and take the screenshot again.
4. A shadow on a view with no background colour is drawn under every child, text included. Give the view a background, or put the shadow on a background view.
5. Measure the spacing: run `axe describe-ui --udid <simulator id>` on each screen and pass the JSON to Eidova's `inspect-spacing` as `nativeStates`. Fix what it reports, then measure again. If AXe is missing, install it with `brew install cameroncooke/axe/axe`, or say that spacing was not measured.

guides.name: get-swiftui-guide
guides.title: SwiftUI
guides.text:
# SwiftUI Guides matching "accessible forms dynamic type"

## Use SwiftUI state and native conventions (46% match)

1. Choose state ownership deliberately: transient view state belongs near the view, while shared models have a stable owner. Preserve identity in repeated and navigated content.
2. Use semantic text styles, native controls and platform navigation. Respect safe areas and avoid fixed heights that clip Dynamic Type content.
3. Provide VoiceOver labels, values and traits. Keep loading, failure and empty data distinct, and cancel view-bound work when it is no longer needed.

Verify: Test the smallest and largest supported text sizes, VoiceOver, rotation and interrupted asynchronous work.

Next: call `find-design-system` with the product's description. If no person is there to choose, take the top match and say which one you took. Then call `get-design-system-kit` to install it.

Check the screen on a device before you report it done:

1. Build the app with the iphonesimulator SDK (`xcodebuild`, or `xcrun swiftc` with an `-ios<version>-simulator` target) and run it in a simulator. A typecheck alone is not a build. If `xcrun` says the iphonesimulator SDK cannot be located, the command line tools are selected instead of Xcode: run the command with `DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer`.
2. Take a screenshot of every state you built: empty, selected, disabled and dark mode.
3. Read each screenshot. Every label shows once and reads clearly: no text drawn twice, no button whose label matches its fill, no clipped or overlapping text, no chart or card spilling over its neighbour. Fix what fails and take the screenshot again.
4. A `.shadow()` on a container with no background is drawn under every child, text included. Put the shadow on the background shape instead.
5. Measure the spacing: run `axe describe-ui --udid <simulator id>` on each screen and pass the JSON to Eidova's `inspect-spacing` as `nativeStates`. Fix what it reports, then measure again. If AXe is missing, install it with `brew install cameroncooke/axe/axe`, or say that spacing was not measured.
6. Where `review-ui-code` is available, send each .swift file path with its complete inline content. Fix every serious finding, then send the files again.

guides.name: get-shopify-guide
guides.title: Shopify
guides.text:
1. Move customer-facing text into locale files using the theme's translation conventions. Preserve interpolation variables and pluralization where the platform supports them.
2. Use Shopify's money and localization objects rather than manually appending currency symbols. Check that variant prices and cart totals use the selected market.
3. Allow longer translated labels and right-to-left layout where supported. Do not embed required copy only in product images.

Verify: Render multiple languages and markets, including long labels, plural quantities and the complete checkout handoff.

1. Run the version of Theme Check appropriate to the project and address syntax, schema and high-impact warnings. A clean static check does not establish working storefront behavior.
2. Verify section editor lifecycle, localization, keyboard controls, product variants, cart updates and responsive layout with representative data.
3. Use a preview theme for review and preserve the merchant's live theme settings. Compare the intended change against the existing page at the same width.

Verify: Keep a preview URL and repeat the affected customer task, including failure and empty states, before publishing.

1. Fit changes into the theme's existing templates, sections, blocks and assets. Use merchant-editable settings for content and design choices that must be maintained without code.
2. Keep product, cart, localization and customer behavior tied to Shopify's actual objects. Do not replace live pricing or inventory with sample values.
3. Support section lifecycle events and theme-editor reloads without duplicate listeners. Preserve header, footer and relevant legal links.

Verify: Add, reorder and remove the section in the editor, then test the storefront with actual product and cart states.

1. Use documented Liquid objects and filters for the current theme context. Escape untrusted text and use the platform's money and localization formatting.
2. Check empty values, collection limits and variant availability before rendering an action. Keep display labels separate from IDs and handles used for behavior.
3. Avoid expensive repeated lookups and preserve the theme's asset-loading conventions. Do not put credentials or privileged API requests into public theme code.

Verify: Run Theme Check and inspect empty, unavailable, localized and long-content examples in the rendered storefront.

1. Choose setting types, defaults and ranges that fit the actual rendering. Keep IDs stable so existing merchant choices are preserved.
2. Provide useful presets and block limits where needed, and use labels a merchant can understand without implementation knowledge.
3. Keep the schema valid JSON and verify current Shopify restrictions. Reflect a missing or empty setting gracefully in the storefront.

Verify: Run Theme Check, add the section from its preset and test defaults, empty values and every exposed setting.

guides.name: get-three-js-guide
guides.title: Three.js
guides.text:
# Three.js Guides matching "performance accessible canvas fallback"

## Build a scene with a purpose and fallback (41% match)

1. Define the information or interaction the scene must communicate, the camera framing and the target device budget before adding objects.
2. Handle resize, device pixel ratio and unavailable WebGL. Provide useful HTML content or a static alternative for essential information.
3. Dispose of owned geometry, material and texture resources and clean up listeners and loops. Keep shared resource lifetimes explicit.

Verify: Resize the canvas, navigate away and return, and test a low-powered device and WebGL failure.

---

## Budget scene resources and frame work (25% match)

1. Measure frame time, draw calls, triangles, texture memory and loading costs. Set budgets for the target device rather than optimizing a desktop-only preview.
2. Reuse geometry and materials, instance repeated objects and choose texture resolution for actual on-screen size. Avoid allocating objects inside a frequent render loop.
3. Use demand rendering when a scene is idle and lower pixel ratio when appropriate. Balance visual quality with readable, responsive interaction.

Verify: Profile representative scenes and repeated mounts, including a slow device, idle state and worst-case interaction.

---

## Plan capability-based WebGPU rendering (33% match)

1. Check browser, renderer and installed Three.js support before adopting WebGPU or node-based materials. Feature detection is more useful than browser-name assumptions.
2. Separate scene behavior from renderer-specific material and compute code. Decide whether a WebGL or static fallback can meet the user's task.
3. Measure shader compilation, memory and frame costs with the chosen renderer. Do not assume a WebGL shader can be moved unchanged into a TSL pipeline.

Verify: Run supported and unsupported capability paths and compare correctness and performance with representative assets.

---

## Use Drei helpers within explicit lifetimes (17% match)

1. Confirm a helper's current API and requirements in the installed version. Use it to solve a specific camera, loading, staging or interaction requirement.
2. Keep camera control ownership clear and avoid multiple controls competing for the same input. Bound resource-heavy helpers and progressive effects.
3. Provide loading/error UI and accessible HTML equivalents for important interactions. Dispose or reuse owned assets deliberately.

Verify: Test loading failure, unmount, multiple scenes and control interactions with touch and a keyboard.

---

## Make shader effects predictable and bounded (17% match)

1. Define the effect's uniforms, coordinate spaces and time source. Keep expensive work and branch behavior consistent with the target hardware budget.
2. Treat shaders as part of a material and color-management pipeline. Check output color space, tone mapping and transparency with the actual renderer configuration.
3. Use a simple material fallback when compilation or capability checks fail. Keep required labels and controls outside the effect.

Verify: Check compile errors, renderer warnings, the intended color pipeline and frame time on representative devices.

Next: call `find-design-system` with the product's description. If no person is there to choose, take the top match and say which one you took. Then call `get-design-system-kit` to install it.

guides.name: get-sales-principle
guides.title: Sales conversations
guides.text:
# Sales Principles matching "clear offer truthful evidence next action"

## Connect the offer to a verified buyer problem (39% match)

1. Ask about the buyer's problem, current approach, decision constraints and cost of leaving the problem unresolved. Confirm your understanding before proposing a solution.
2. Connect each relevant capability to a supported outcome. State limitations and avoid invented customer references, metrics or urgency.
3. Agree on a practical next step, owner and date. Make price, scope and commitments clear before asking for a decision.

Verify: Check that the proposal uses the buyer's actual requirements and that every material claim has support.

---

## Help a buyer explain the decision internally (44% match)

1. Understand who evaluates value, risk, procurement and implementation. Give the champion a concise statement of the problem, proposal, evidence and unresolved questions.
2. Provide truthful comparisons, clear pricing and an implementation plan with responsibilities. Do not invent stakeholder approval or financial returns.
3. Make supporting material easy to share and verify. Offer answers to likely concerns without asking the champion to hide limitations.

Verify: Check that an uninvolved stakeholder can understand the recommendation and verify its important claims.

---

## Clarify an objection before responding (33% match)

1. Acknowledge the concern and ask what specifically makes the choice difficult. Distinguish price, fit, risk, timing and decision authority instead of delivering a generic rebuttal.
2. Respond with relevant evidence or a concrete scope adjustment. Do not claim that every objection is secretly interest or pressure the buyer to ignore a valid limitation.
3. Confirm whether the answer resolves the concern and identify a useful next step, including declining the offer when the fit is wrong.

Verify: Restate the buyer's concern accurately and identify what evidence or change would actually address it.

---

## Translate capabilities into useful outcomes (11% match)

1. Start from a task the buyer actually performs, explain the capability that changes it and identify the resulting benefit.
2. Distinguish a product fact from a predicted effect. Quantify only when the input and calculation are known, and show the assumptions.
3. Omit capabilities unrelated to the decision. A short proposal tied to real requirements is more useful than an undifferentiated feature list.

Verify: For each proposed capability, name the buyer task it helps and the evidence supporting the claimed outcome.
